entries.topic: IOR: origins, statutes, governance, clients, 2024 and 2025 results, dividend, 2022 rescript and 2025 Coniuncta Cura

claims.text: Leo XIII established the Commission ad pias causas in 1887, which became the Administration for the Works of Religion; Pius XII approved its statutes on 17 March 1941 and by chirograph of 27 June 1942 founded the Institute for the Works of Religion with juridical personality, incorporating the Administration; John Paul II gave it a new framework on 1 March 1990.

Under its statutes the IOR's purpose is the custody and administration of movable and immovable goods transferred or entrusted to it by physical or juridical persons and intended for works of religion or charity.

Organs: Commission of Cardinals (five cardinals, five-year term renewable once); Prelate; Board of Superintendence (seven members, five-year term, its President is legal representative); Director General appointed by the Board with Commission approval; external auditor appointed by the Commission for three years renewable once. Statutes renewed ad experimentum 8 Aug 2019 and definitively 30 Jan 2023.

Reporting on the 2014 results (May 2015), AP said the IOR had closed about 4,600 accounts that were dormant or outside its revised client base, which was limited to religious communities, Catholic bodies, clergy, current and former Vatican staff, and embassies and diplomats accredited to the Holy See; 15,181 account holders remained.

IOR 2024: net profit EUR 32.8m (+7%); dividend EUR 13.8m to the Holy Father resolved by the Commission of Cardinals; net equity EUR 731.9m; Tier 1 ratio 69.43%; client assets EUR 5.7bn (2023: EUR 5.4bn) covering deposits, current accounts, asset management and custody; over 12,000 clients in more than 110 countries; audited by Mazars, approved by the Board 29 April 2025.

IOR 2025 (report 11 May 2026): net income EUR 51m (+55.5%, highest in ten years); dividend EUR 24.3m to the Holy Father (+76.1%); client assets EUR 5.9bn; net assets EUR 815.3m; Tier 1 71.9%; about 12,000 clients in more than 110 countries; 115 employees; Deloitte clean opinion; Board approved 28 April 2026; de Franssu's term ended and François Pauly took office as President.

Rescript of 23 August 2022 interpreted Praedicate Evangelium art. 219 §3 to make the IOR exclusively responsible as manager and custodian of the Holy See's movable assets; funds in other banks to be moved within 30 days of 1 September 2022.

Leo XIV's rescript Coniuncta Cura (reported 6 October 2025) repealed the 2022 exclusivity: APSA should generally use the IOR but may use foreign intermediaries if competent bodies deem it more efficient or convenient, under the policies of the investment committee chaired by Cardinal Kevin Farrell.

entries.topic: APSA 1967 founding, 2020-2025 reports, Secretariat of State transfer; Governorate and museums; Holy See consolidated statements; pension fund

claims.text: Paul VI established APSA on 15 August 1967 by the apostolic constitution Regimini Ecclesiae Universae; its Extraordinary Section took over the Special Administration that Pius XI created in June 1929 to manage the funds Italy paid under the Lateran Financial Convention. Under Praedicate Evangelium (2022) APSA administers the Holy See's movable and immovable patrimony; financial operations run through the IOR.

Motu proprio of 26 December 2020: from 1 January 2021 ownership of the Secretariat of State's funds, bank accounts, investments, shareholdings and real estate passed to APSA; liquid assets to be transferred by 4 February 2021; Peter's Pence placed as a sub-account of the Papal Funds administered by APSA; Secretariat for the Economy given control.

APSA's first public budget (released July 2021, for 2020) listed about 4,051 properties in Italy and about 1,120 abroad; about 14% of Italian properties rented at market rates; Holy See deficit EUR 64.8m in 2020 (79.2m in 2019).

APSA 2021: surplus EUR 8.11m; EUR 30m to the Curia. 2022: break-even with EUR 32.27m contribution. 2023: surplus EUR 45.9m, contribution EUR 37.9m; 4,249 units in Italy and about 1,200 abroad and through subsidiaries (London, Paris, Geneva, Lausanne); 19.2% at market rent, 10.4% subsidised, 70.4% at zero rent.

APSA 2024: profit EUR 62.2m; contribution EUR 46.087m (30m fixed + 16.087m variable); Curia financial needs EUR 170.4m; 4,234 units in Italy (2,866 owned by APSA incl. 1,367 residential and 395 commercial; 1,368 belonging to other bodies); foreign companies British Grolux Investments, Sopridex, Profima; EUR 6m IMU and EUR 3.19m IRES paid to Italy.

APSA 2025: operating result EUR 22.8m; contribution to the Holy See EUR 22.7m; net equity EUR 2,686m (2024: 2,597.5m) after gold (+40.8m), property (+39.2m) and securities (+16.3m) revaluations; total assets EUR 3,337.5m; investment property EUR 2,211m; 4,281 units in Italy (2,945 own, 1,336 of other Holy See entities) and about 1,200 abroad; gold 29% of own portfolio.

Holy See consolidated 2024: operating income EUR 1,230.7m, operating expenses EUR 1,275.2m, surplus EUR 1.6m (2023 deficit 51.2m); operating deficit EUR 44.4m; total assets EUR 6,326.7m; net equity EUR 4,277.0m; excluding hospitals revenue 546.5m and expenses 527.8m; apostolic mission spending EUR 393.3m; Governorate contributed EUR 20.0m (2023: 15.0m). The statements give no valuation of historic or artistic heritage.

Secretariat for the Economy, 2015 consolidated accounts (released 4 March 2017): Holy See deficit EUR 12.4m; IOR contribution EUR 50m; canon 1271 contributions EUR 24m; Governorate surplus EUR 59.9m driven mainly by the Museums; first accounts under the VFMP (IPSAS-based).

On 21 November 2024 Francis wrote that an analysis showed 'a serious prospective imbalance' in the Vatican pension fund and named Cardinal Kevin Farrell special administrator; the lay employees' association asked for the fund's balance sheet to be published.

Vatican Museums full ticket EUR 20 from 1 January 2024 (reduced EUR 8). Quotidiano Nazionale reported about 6.9 million visitors in 2025. CWR (May 2020) estimated at least $120m a year from ordinary tickets (estimate, not an official figure).

entries.topic: Peter's Pence: purpose, 2020-2025 reports, London sale

claims.text: Guerrero (25 June 2021): Peter's Pence supports both the pope's charity and the Holy See's mission (dicasteries that generate little or no income); 2020 collection EUR 44.1m; London losses 'did not weigh on' the Peter's Pence fund but on other Secretariat of State funds; fund held about EUR 205m at end-2020, partly in illiquid investments including the London building.

2021: contributions about EUR 46.9m; disbursements about EUR 65.3m, of which about EUR 55.5m to Vatican departments, embassies, communications and local churches and about EUR 10m to 157 direct-assistance projects; deficit covered by other income (Reuters).
The London building was sold to Bain Capital for GBP 186m (announced 1 July 2022); the capital loss was transferred to the Secretariat of State's reserve funds; Peter's Pence 'has not been touched'.

2023: income EUR 52m (donations 48.4m, financial 3.6m); 2022 income EUR 107m including a capital gain on the sale of fund real estate; expenditure EUR 109.4m; EUR 90m to the apostolic mission through 68 Holy See bodies; EUR 13m to 236 projects in 76 countries; US 28.1% of donations.

2024: income EUR 58m (donations 54.3m, other 3.7m); expenditure EUR 75.4m; EUR 61.2m to dicasteries (about 17% of the Holy See's EUR 367.4m mission costs); EUR 13.3m to 239 projects in 66 countries; donors US 25.2%, France 15%, Italy 5.2%, Brazil 3%, Germany 2.8%.

2025: revenue EUR 57.6m (donations 54.5m); expenditure EUR 59.8m; deficit EUR 2.2m attributed to exchange rates; EUR 41.2m to the Holy See's mission (about 10% of EUR 404.5m mission spending); EUR 13.3m to 252 projects in 74 countries; dioceses 63.6% of donations; United States EUR 14.2m.

entries.topic: What is on and off the books: canon law ownership, heritage at symbolic value, origins of the $73bn and 177 million acre figures

claims.text: Canon 1256: under the supreme authority of the Roman Pontiff, ownership of goods belongs to the juridic person that lawfully acquired them; canon 1273: the pope is supreme administrator and steward of all ecclesiastical goods; canon 1271: bishops are to help supply the Apostolic See's needs according to their dioceses' means.
In 2005 AP reported that St Peter's Basilica and the Sistine Chapel were listed at a symbolic one euro each in the Holy See's accounts, its other real estate at about EUR 700m; 2003 deficit $11.8m.

Marketplace (Feb 2023) put Catholic Church assets at 'at least $73 billion' by adding estimates for Australian and German dioceses, Trinity Church in New York, the IOR and the Holy See, noting dioceses are separate and the true figure unknown; it quoted a 2004 Vatican accountant that the basilica and chapel were listed at a symbolic 1 euro; Posner put global Church property at about 277,000 square miles with no official valuation.
Trinity Church Wall Street, with a portfolio of about $6bn, is an Episcopal parish.

The '177 million acres' figure circulates through Bisnow (2015, citing a 2011 Business Insider list) and Benzinga (2022) without a stated method; David Owen in the New Yorker (2021) estimated about 200 million acres; Burhans found no comprehensive Church land inventory.

entries.topic: Audit verification of Peter's Pence and APSA 2025 details

claims.text: Peter's Pence 2023: offerings EUR 48.4m, of which dioceses EUR 31.2m (64.4%), foundations EUR 13.9m, private donors EUR 2.1m, religious orders EUR 1.2m; by country United States EUR 13.6m (28.1%), Italy EUR 3.1m (6.4%), Brazil EUR 1.9m (3.9%); disbursements EUR 103m (EUR 90m mission, EUR 13m direct aid). Percentages are shares of offerings.

Peter's Pence 2025 report published 30 June 2026: donations EUR 54.5m (dioceses EUR 34.7m, 63.6%; foundations EUR 13m; private donors EUR 5.4m; religious institutes EUR 1.4m); United States EUR 14.2m; Africa EUR 5.2m for 73 projects; income EUR 57.6m, expenses EUR 59.8m, deficit EUR 2.2m attributed to foreign-exchange fluctuations.

APSA 2025: Piccinotti called 2024 'un esercizio straordinario e non ripetibile' and 2025 'il ritorno a condizioni operative ordinarie'; about EUR 16m of realised portfolio gains were booked to net equity under the Vatican Financial Management Policy rather than the income statement.
IOR account review: about 4,600 accounts closed by end-2014 (AP, ANSA) and about 4,800 in all by the review's completion in October 2015 (AIF 2015 report).
